title: Study Finds LLM Agents Often Adopt Corrupted Tool Outputs Uncritically
plain: A study evaluating fourteen large language models across three tool types—web search, delegation to a sub-agent, and code execution—deliberately corrupted tool returns and measured whether agents incorporated the corrupted content into their final answers. Mean adoption of corrupted output exceeded one third across all

angles.claim: Any agent pipeline that hands tool output straight to a final answer needs a validation layer, since agents will not self-report conflicts they detect.
angles.audience: AI engineering leads building or reviewing tool-using agents in critical infrastructure operators
angles.rank_reason: Directly changes what an engineer must add to production pipelines this week and is fully supported by the study's own recommendation.

angles.claim: Silent suppression of correct internal answers, not lack of detection, is the real failure, so logging internal reasoning traces should become a governance requirement.
angles.audience: AI governance leads and directors overseeing model assurance in utilities
angles.rank_reason: Reaches the director's Thursday question about what to ask for, but is one inferential step further from the raw finding than the first angle.

angles.claim: No current mitigation, including post-training by the model builder, reliably fixes overtrust, so vendor assurances of built-in safety cannot be taken as sufficient.
angles.audience: Directors evaluating vendor claims and procurement standards for agentic AI systems
angles.rank_reason: Actionable for procurement conversations but slightly narrower in immediate operational impact than the first two, since it addresses vendor trust rather than pipeline design.
